text:
Priya (Support): hey team, escalating a customer complaint — they say after a traffic spike their requests started getting 429s and much higher tail latency. customer: acme-fintech, project=acme-prod, model=redwood-4x, region=us-west. request_id from their logs: r-0a1b2c3d4e. started ~2026-03-10T18:05Z. they think it's "perceived throttling" when they send short, very bursty inference calls (many concurrent reqs with ~16 token responses).

Priya (Support): errors they see: mostly 429 Too Many Requests, a few 503 Gateway Timeout, and a lot of responses that complete but with 200+ms extra latency vs baseline (baseline is ~35-50ms). they included this header snippet from a failing call: 
```
x-request-id: r-0a1b2c3d4e
x-rate-limit-remaining: 0
x-rate-limit-reset: 2026-03-10T18:06:40Z
x-server-latency-ms: 312
x-batch-size: 8
```

Jordan (SRE): thanks @Priya — can you paste the exact curl or the repro loop they used? also need the SDK / API client version. if we can reproduce we can check the router/backpressure metrics.

Priya (Support): they use our Python SDK v1.11.2 and call chat.completions with concurrency=40 from a k8s job. here's the simplified repro they shared: 
```
# customer-provided repro (50 concurrent workers)
for i in $(seq 1 200); do
  curl -sS -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat.completions \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{"model":"redwood-4x","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"short prompt"}],"max_tokens":16}' &
done
wait
```

Priya (Support): they said swaps to dedicated capacity reduced 429s but they still see intermittent latency spikes. they suspect KV cache or batching is introducing queuing. any ideas?

Sam (Eng-runtime): this is a classic interaction: continuous batching + small responses + KV cache can look like throttling. a few points: 1) continuous batcher will hold an incoming request up to max_batch_wait_ms to try to form bigger batches; during a sustained high concurrency burst that manifests as queueing inside the router. 2) KV cache hits reduce token generation time but can increase per-request variance (if some requests hit the cache and others miss, the overall batch runtime is uneven). 3) when x-rate-limit-remaining hits 0 we return 429s, but we also have per-route inflight limits which will queue or backpressure long before token quota exhaustion.

Sam (Eng-runtime): repro guidance and quick checks: capture these headers from their client requests (we already have x-request-id): 
- x-rate-limit-remaining
- x-rate-limit-reset
- x-batch-size (we add this when a request is batched)
- x-kv-cache-hit: true|false (we log a per-request marker when KV prefix cache is hit)
- x-router-queue-ms (how long it waited in the router queue)

Jordan (SRE): to help triage please ask them to run this concurrent test with tracing headers enabled (we can attach to request_ids). also ask them to set SDK env var REDWOOD_DEBUG=true. here is a small script to reproduce locally (concurrency and qps knobs): 
```
# repro.sh
CONCURRENCY=40
REQS=400
for i in $(seq 1 $REQS); do
  python -c "import requests,os; print(requests.post('https://api.redwood.example/v1/chat.completions', headers={'Authorization':'Bearer '+os.getenv('TOKEN'),'X-Debug':'1'}, json={'model':'redwood-4x','messages':[{'role':'user','content':'hi'}],'max_tokens':16}).headers)" &
  if (( i % CONCURRENCY == 0 )); then sleep 0.1; fi
done
wait
```

Devon (ML Eng): couple of knobs we can adjust quickly on runtime side: 
- reduce max_batch_wait_ms to 5-10ms for latency-sensitive small responses (default might be 50ms).
- lower max_batch_size to avoid big variance when KV hits are uneven.
- enable prefer_small_batches for that customer route if they want lower p99s.
- disable continuous batching entirely for <20-token responses (not ideal for cost but fixes perceived throttling).

Devon (ML Eng): config example (for eng team): 
```
{
  "route": "acme-prod",
  "batching": {
    "enabled": true,
    "max_batch_wait_ms": 10,
    "max_batch_size": 16,
    "prefer_small_batches": true
  },
  "kv_cache": {
    "enabled": true,
    "prefix_cache_ttl_s": 3600
  }
}
```

Priya (Support): great. customer asked if KV cache evictions could cause a sudden wave of higher latency that looks like throttling if many requests fall back to compute at once?

Sam (Eng-runtime): yes. if their prefix cache TTL is short or their distribution of prompts is wide, you'll see simultaneous cache misses which increase compute time per item in a batch — the batch takes longer, the router sees longer occupancy and that reduces throughput, which can look like throttling to callers. also, cache warm-up on scale events (e.g., new replica) can create spikes.

Priya (Support): billing/quotas angle — customer says they didn't exceed monthly token allotment. could there still be per-minute or per-route quota triggers causing 429s?

Luis (Billing): yes. we enforce both token/usage billing quotas and rate limits. monthly tokens could be fine but they might hit per-minute or per-second soft caps. check the project quota page and the headers; x-rate-limit-remaining is zero in their header snippet which is the smoking gun. we can bump their per-minute QPS but they should also consider smoothing bursts via client-side jitter/backoff.

Luis (Billing): our rate-limit header mapping: 
- x-rate-limit-remaining: integer tokens/requests left in window
- x-rate-limit-reset: ISO timestamp when window resets
- x-quota-remaining: remaining monthly token quota
If x-rate-limit-remaining==0 -> 429 from server. we can open a quota increase request but need expected sustained QPS numbers.

Jordan (SRE): operational ask: @OncallBot please collect router traces and batcher metrics for request_id r-0a1b2c3d4e and time window 2026-03-10T18:04Z..18:08Z. include per-replica queue length, batch sizes, and kv_cache-hit ratio.

OncallBot: acknowledged — collecting traces, ETA ~3m. (automated: trace collection id t-9f8e7d6c)

Priya (Support): follow-ups for customer: 1) run the repro with REDWOOD_DEBUG to capture headers and attach logs 2) try client-side smoothing (random jitter between bursts) and lower concurrency to see if 429s disappear 3) we can toggle max_batch_wait_ms for their route as an experiment or migrate them to a dedicated pool. Which should we propose first?

Sam (Eng-runtime): recommend experiment order: 1) client smoothing/backoff (lowest effort) 2) temporary route-level batcher config (set max_batch_wait_ms=10, prefer_small_batches true) 3) if still bad, trial on dedicated capacity.

Devon (ML Eng): also suggest adding a lightweight local cache for repeated prefixes on their side so backend KV cache is more effective.

Priya (Support): I'll send these steps and ask them to attach REDWOOD_DEBUG output and a few x-request-id values. I'll also offer to open a quota increase ticket if they provide steady QPS.

Luis (Billing): please include expected sustained QPS and burst size in the ticket. Finance will escalate if they want a month-over-month commit.

Sam (Eng-runtime): one last note — if they see many 200 responses with x-batch-size > 1 and high x-server-latency-ms, that's evidence the batcher held requests too long. if so we should tune batcher rather than increase quota.

Priya (Support): thanks all — action items: (1) I will ask customer for REDWOOD_DEBUG logs + sample x-request-ids (2) Jordan/Oncall to pull router/batcher traces for r-0a1b2c3d4e (3) Devon/Sam to prepare a route config patch we can toggle for them (4) Luis to prep quota increase form if customer requests it. tagging for visibility :thumbsup:
